context: plot-by-plot repetition · site infrastructure & utility enablement

brief.intro: New to this project type? A residential compound is many near-identical low-rise villas or townhouses built in parallel across a serviced plot, tied together by shared site infrastructure — roads, utility networks, a perimeter wall and communal amenities. Unlike a single house, the schedule isn't driven by any one unit's complexity; it's driven by production rate — how many units per week move through each construction stage — and by whether infrastructure is ready ahead of the units it serves. The programme is really two schedules running together: a horizontal infrastructure schedule (roads, utility trunks, boundary works) and a repeating per-unit finishing cycle that rolls across the plots behind it. A late road or utility corridor blocks access to whole clusters of units, so infrastructure is planned ahead of the unit wave, not behind it, and handover is normally phased villa-by-villa or cluster-by-cluster rather than on one single date.

scope.name: Enabling & site infrastructure
scope.desc: Earthworks, main and internal roads, and utility trunk networks (water, sewer, power, telecom) built ahead of the unit wave.

scope.name: Boundary & security works
scope.desc: Perimeter wall/fencing, gatehouse and community security systems.

scope.name: Per-unit structure
scope.desc: Foundations, blockwork/frame and roof for each villa or townhouse type across the plot.

scope.name: Per-unit MEP first & second fix
scope.desc: Plumbing, electrical and HVAC rough-in and trim-out, repeated per unit.

scope.name: Per-unit finishing
scope.desc: Waterproofing, screed, tiling, paint, joinery and sanitary fixtures, repeated per unit.

scope.name: External works per plot
scope.desc: Boundary walls, driveways and external render/waterproofing around each unit.

scope.name: Common amenities
scope.desc: Clubhouse, pools and landscaped communal areas, where included in scope.

scope.name: Utility energisation
scope.desc: Power, water and telecom connection and metering per cluster of units.

scope.name: Snagging & phased handover
scope.desc: Defect inspection and handover, released villa-by-villa or cluster-by-cluster.

must_get_right: Sequence infrastructure ahead of the unit wave — a road or utility trunk not ready on time blocks every unit behind it.
Plan around production rate, not one villa's logic — the programme lives or dies on units-per-week, so protect crew continuity across plots.
Phase the handover into clusters so utility energisation, snagging and handover happen predictably rather than all at once.
Keep common works (landscaping, amenities, boundary wall) visible on the schedule — they're often done last and can quietly become the tail of the whole programme.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Because units repeat, a typical-unit fragnet is built once per unit type and replicated across each cluster/phase rather than modelled activity-by-activity for every plot.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard local working week for finishing trades; enabling infrastructure and roads run on a continuous calendar ahead of unit release so they never become the constraint. A weather allowance is embedded for earthworks and external works.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs enabling infrastructure & main roads → utility trunk to each cluster → structure wave → MEP → finishing wave → energisation → phased handover. This is better read as a critical chain than a single critical path: the constraint is the slowest repeating trade's production rate, not any one unit's logic.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen per unit type before release; land handover and enabling works are complete ahead of the unit wave; authority approvals for infrastructure are obtained per phase; a single continuous mobilisation across the site.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Multiple simultaneous fronts across a large plot require crew-mobility and material-laydown planning; production rate is resource-constrained — finishing crews are typically the bottleneck; common amenities often compete for the same late-stage trade resources as the unit wave.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: infrastructure delay blocking unit access, finishing-crew productivity below plan slowing the wave, and late design changes to common amenities. Contingency is held at cluster boundaries so slippage doesn't cascade and phased handover dates stay achievable.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (cluster/phase handover milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 per cluster; expanded to Level 4 per unit for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
